All coated samples exhibit biphasic kinetics: an initial rapid phase (0-5 min) followed by a slower diffusion-limited phase that becomes more pronounced with increasing solution volume. This behavior reflects sequential transport through two domains: the ultrathin PA coating (~20 nm) at pore mouths and the amine-filled mesoporous network (~10 nm pores, several μm depth). For such sequential resistances, the overall rate is governed by the slower step. Given the ultrathin nature of the coating relative to the pore depth, and the high viscosity of the amine-filled pores, diffusion through the amine-filled pore network likely dominates the overall transport kinetics rather than passage through the coating itself. This is consistent with the observation that the kinetic penalty scales with solution volume (T1-1x < T1-2x < T1-4x): increased solution volume produces more extensive coating coverage and reduced amine loading per particle (as evidenced by TGA, Figure 15b), which may decrease the effective amine accessibility and increase the average diffusion path length within the pore network. The modest kinetic penalties (2.1-2.9x 23 slower) relative to the substantial stability improvements (18-fold for T1-4x) indicate that the coating strategy successfully balances protection with CO transport efficiency. 2 The progressive kinetic penalty with increasing solution volume (T1-1x: 2.1x, T1-2x: 2.4x, T1-4x: 2.9x slower) correlates with the increased PA content observed in TGA analysis (Figure 15c). The more pronounced PA decomposition features in T1-4x compared to T1-1x suggest greater overall coating mass and potentially more extensive pore mouth coverage. This enhanced coating coverage, while beneficial for amine retention, increases the diffusional resistance for CO 2 transport to amine sites within the pores. The biphasic kinetics becomes more pronounced at higher solution volumes, consistent with more complete pore mouth encapsulation that restricts gas access to the internal amine-filled pore network. The trade-off between stability (improved by more complete coating) and kinetics (slowed by increased diffusion resistance) is evident in the systematic trends across T1-1x, T1-2x, and T1-4x. While T1-4x achieves excellent stability (>97% retention), the 2.9-fold kinetic penalty makes it less attractive for applications requiring rapid cycling. Effect of TMC concentration at constant TMC: TAPA molar ratio (1.83:1): (c) cycling stability and (d) time to reach 95% capacity. All samples compared to uncoated TAPA/SBA-15 control. Figure 17a shows T2-0.5x achieves superior stability: 1.33 to 1.31 mmol g-1 (1.5% loss), a 27-fold improvement and best performance among all samples. T10-0.1x shows poor stability: 1.62 to 1.14 mmol g-1 (29.5% loss), barely better than uncoated. The divergence despite identical TMC:TAPA mass ratios reveals local TMC concentration critically affects coating defect formation.
